question: For the Proxima Bank 429 spike after priority routing rollout, what caused the throttling and what temporary policy exception did we apply, and how do we verify it is not burning the enterprise route SLOs?
answer: The 429s were caused by overload/admission control during regional pressure: Proxima’s combined chat + embeddings bursts exceeded the enterprise route budget / conservative burst multiplier, so the system shed or throttled them to protect enterprise SLOs. We applied a time-boxed temporary burst exception for PROXIMA-ENT-014 on chat+embeddings in us-east, with a 14-day expiry, monitoring annotation, and automatic rollback if enterprise p99 latency burn or sustained shed rate exceeded threshold. To verify it is not burning enterprise route SLOs, check the enterprise p95/p99 latency and the enterprise route SLO error-budget burn dashboards, plus 429 rate by reason code and queue depth/scheduler lag during canary/post-change monitoring.

question: What is the procedure for an emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release (Hosted and Dedicated)?
answer:
Emergency rollback procedure:
1) Declare/confirm an incident, identify the prior known-good runtime release tag, and assign IC/Runtime oncall/Release-Infra oncall/SRE roles.
2) Freeze the rollout immediately so no further canary or progressive expansion occurs.
3) Hosted: pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then roll back in order: any non-critical region still on canary, the remaining canary cohort, then all regions on the bad release. After each region, verify 5xx normalizes, GPU utilization returns to expected, and TTFT/token throughput recover.
4) Dedicated: identify impacted clusters/tenants, then execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure. For high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate comms/approvals via CS and the emergency change policy.
5) Keep the incident open until stability holds for 30 minutes on Hosted and 60 minutes on Dedicated; confirm latency returns to baseline, no new error modes appear, and autoscaling stabilizes.
6) Capture rollback job links, affected regions/clusters, dashboard permalinks/screenshots, and customer comms.

citations.quote: This runbook describes how to perform an emergency rollback of the Serving Runtime release across Hosted and Dedicated fleets.

Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes: p95 time-to-first-token (TTFT) regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes; error rate > 2% on generation routes due to runtime (5xx, timeouts, OOM); canary cohort shows sustained degradation and traffic shift cannot be halted cleanly; repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build.

An incident has been declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely; Runtime oncall has identified candidate rollback target; Release engineer or infra oncall is available to execute the pipeline rollback.

Incident Commander (IC): owns the decision to rollback and comms cadence. Runtime oncall: validates technical root cause hypothesis and rollback target. Release/Infra oncall: executes the rollback in deployment tooling. SRE: monitors fleet-level SLOs and regional health signals.

Pause it immediately. Hosted rollback: pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then roll back in this order: non-critical region, remaining canary cohort, all regions on the bad release. After each region completes, verify 5xx rate normalizes, GPU utilization returns to expected, TTFT and token/s recover to baseline. Dedicated rollback: identify impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants, execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure; for high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for outbound comms and approvals.

Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated); confirm request latency distributions return to baseline and no new error modes appear; ensure autoscaling stabilizes.

If rollback target also shows elevated OOMs, stop and reassess... If only one model family is impacted, consider temporarily routing to a compatible variant instead of fleet rollback... Avoid rapid flip-flopping between releases.

Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes:

summary: Post-launch review of Hot-route capacity protection GA in us-east and eu-west regions for /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings, and /v1/rerank routes. Compares 14 days pre-GA vs. 14 days post-GA, analyzing incident rate, tail latency, and shed behavior for enterprise-priority and best-effort tiers. Key findings include successful enterprise traffic protection with stable latency and request success during bursts, but spiky best-effort shedding due to config sensitivity and a reason code mismatch edge case in 429 responses. Identified observability gaps for identifying top customer traffic contributors and need for further validation of streaming client behavior. Follow-up actions include per-region threshold tuning, unifying 429 reason codes, implementing a two-signal confirmation for shedding, developing an internal top contributors troubleshooting view, and creating an SDK streaming regression test matrix.
